title: A Generation Revolts
content: Across Europe, young people are being arrested in their thousands. In Milan, jackbooted soldiers from the Italian military — average age, 38 — haul protesters, some of whom are as young as 12 and 13, away from picket lines and into armored vehicles. Italy’s government — average age, 60 — has passed a new decree allowing detainments for up to 24 hours without charge. Vandals can now be arrested 48 hours after their crimes; Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, 53, has called for their parents to face financial penalties too.

title: When AIs Become Unruly Swarms
content:
In a harbor before dawn, a hundred fishing boats prepare to leave in the dark of the morning. Nets are checked, and ropes loosened. As the boats reach open water, a voice breaks through the radio static: “Abort. Whales sighted.” The majority of the boats, 90 of them, turn back. Some captains cannot fathom inflicting pain on the creatures. Others fear a fine. Through their binoculars, they look for a glimpse of the pod. Instead, they see the remaining 10 boats continuing toward the fishing grounds. Did they miss the warning? Did they doubt it? Or did they care more about what they stand to gain?

By afternoon, the 10 boats return with their catch. The others are still tied to the quay, their holds empty. Their shared waters rewarded bad behavior. Next time, how many will still turn back?

title: Serbia’s Experiment: Combining Democracy & Meritocracy
content:
It is no less true for being a cliché that innovation comes mostly from the edges. Whether in politics, markets or technology, fresh approaches emerge from the periphery and the margins rather than the well-established core. When it comes to the governing practices and institutions of democracies, innovation tends also to arrive not from the mature states, but the fledgling ones, less bound by legacy structures and entrenched constituencies.

That is the case today in Serbia, which only became a sovereign state in its own right in 2006 after its split from Montenegro following the breakup of Cold War-era Yugoslavia that began unraveling in 1992.

For the last 14 years, it has been ruled by a corrupt autocrat, Aleksandr Vučić, in the mold of Hungary’s Viktor Orbán. When his regime became too much to bear, a revolt by the nation’s youth erupted. The straw that broke the camel’s back came in November 2024 when the concrete canopy of a train station in Novi Sad collapsed and killed 16 people. Its shoddy construction was blamed on corruption in building permits and lax oversight inspections.

title: Democrats Should Not Revert To The Status Quo Ante
content:
The great blue wave that washed over America in the election should not lure Democrats into the delusion that they are once again lovingly embraced by the body politic.

Rather, it should be seen for what it is: a widespread counter-revolt at the ballot box against all that Trumpism has wrought — a heightened crisis of affordability exacerbated by trade wars and a war of choice with Iran, self-dealing corruption, politicization of the rule of law and an unbounded, mean-spirited mega-megalomania rarely seen in mature democracies.

The worst mistake Democrats can make is to misread their mandate. That mandate is to narrow the margin of maneuver of a wounded lame-duck presidency, derail the trajectory toward autocracy and clean up the mess. It is not to return to the status quo ante of cultural elitism, censorious identity politics, lax borders and hyper-globalization that opened the path to Trumpism in the first place.

creator: Nathan Gardels

title: How Aristotle Anticipated The AI Era
content:
“If every instrument could accomplish its own work, obeying or anticipating the will of others,” Aristotle wrote in “Politics” around 350 B.C.E., “if the shuttle would weave and the plectrum touch the lyre without a hand to guide them, chief workmen would not need servants, nor masters slaves.”

For centuries, this passage was understood primarily as a philosophical allegory. Today, what is striking is not Aristotle’s technical imagination but his political imagination. He was more interested in the social consequences of self-operating machines than in their feasibility.

Artificial intelligence forces us to confront this issue anew: What becomes of a society whose economy, purpose and welfare state are built on wage labor if wage labor loses that foundational role? Perhaps the true AI revolution will begin in our conception of what it means to be human, not inside Silicon Valley’s data centers.

title: In Praise Of Japan’s Failure To Keep Up
content:
TOKYO — Nothing triggers the bog-walloping Fenian in me quite like a visit to the British Embassy. This one, with its fine Georgian-revival facade, looked on my last visit a decade ago like a lost Cotswold manor-house brought to life in Tokyo.

But what was it that I found so unsettling? Perhaps the stately setting? Or its gilt-framed displays of a preternaturally regal, late queen? Her gaze following me about the room as I moved among the fine art and mahogany, like those creepy Sacred Heart of Jesus portraits I grew up with. Me, a lad reared in an Irish republican home where the Queen’s annual Christmas messages were as welcome as a poltergeist.

To the more clubbable, the embassy’s English country house manner would have seemed merely civilized; a demonstration that Merrie England had acquired over generations the ability to arrange the upholstery without the aid of an AI shepherd.

title: The Sediment Of Culture Shapes Political Order
content:
As a global journal of ideas, Noema receives feedback from readers all over the world that broadens our way of seeing and kindles the further iteration of our thinking. One recent case is a response by Carl Gay, an executive of the Cloudspago consultancy in Australia, to the Noema essay “When The Present Eats The Future: The Achilles Heel of Consumer Democracies.”

In that essay, I contrast post-Mao China’s capacity for reaching a consensus on long-term goals and determinedly implementing them over many years without a break in continuity with the increasing inability of consumer democracies to do so. The example I used in the context of climate change was how China set the goal decades ago of dominating green technology, especially electric vehicles and batteries, and has steadily achieved that objective, while most open societies of the West have sputtered behind. Its “whole dragon” approach brings the resources of the entire system to bear on the challenge at hand.

title: A New Dawn For Mathematical Progress
content: In the past few months, unreleased frontier AI systems have significantly disrupted a classic conception of mathematics. They successfully established a complete formalization of Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, found a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem and — just a few days ago — generated hundreds of manuscripts that each purport to prove an important mathematical problem. Most recently, on October 26, another of the Clay Millennium Prize problems was felled by an AI system.

title: Turbulent Times Call For Experimental Law
content:
MUNICH — Shortly after wandering into the Munich Urban Colab this summer, I found myself trying to follow an intense conversation in German about the city’s new experiment with autonomous buses. A local official, clocking my curious puzzlement, offered an aside in English: “We are asking ourselves: ‘What does it mean when the law is an experiment too?’”

No question may be more essential to governance in our era of dangerous uncertainty. 

Global warming is accelerating faster than global treaties on mitigation can be negotiated. Climate catastrophes occur with a sudden ferocity beyond what current adaptation laws anticipate. Biological threats surface and kill before public health responses can be formulated. And AI is evolving faster and more wildly than regulators or lawmakers, or even its designers, expect.

All this dizzying unpredictability is undermining traditional legal structures. The threat is not just to the rule of law, but to the very nature of law, at least as humans have conceived it.

title: Noema’s AI Reading List
content:
AI’s climb up the capability ladder is moving more rapidly, even exponentially, than its progenitors expected. To keep up and put it in perspective, Noema has compiled a reading list of our best essays and interviews from a couple of years ago through the present. No doubt, we will need a new list again a few months down the road.

For now, here is a resource for following the trajectory of the most important technological breakthrough of this century so far.

1. How To Future-Proof Your Career In The Age Of AI

The most prized workers will be those who can decode a sea of outputs, spot the meaningful signal and translate it into action that others understand and trust.

by Nils Gilman

2. Whose AI Will Rule The World

As AI changes everything, the Chinese seem more optimistic than the Americans. Why?

by Jacob Dreyer

3. How AI Will Change Us

When the most patient, well-read, emotionally responsive conversationalist in the world is always available, what will we still need from one another?

by Houda Nait El Barj

4. AI Could Actually Help Rebuild The Middle Class

AI doesn’t have to be a job destroyer. It offers us the opportunity to extend expertise to a larger set of workers.

by David Autor
